analysis.one_liner: Backstops pensions in failing union multiemployer retirement plans with federal money and restores benefit cuts.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 42 senators signed on, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let deeply underfunded multiemployer pension plans — mostly union plans covering retired workers — receive unlimited federal aid through the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, with no repayment required, so plans can keep paying full benefits for 30 years. Plans getting aid would have to restore benefits that had been cut under prior federal approval, with back payments to retirees. It would also stop future benefit-cut approvals, extend plan funding timelines, and raise the PBGC's guaranteed benefit floor for multiemployer plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and workers in distressed multiemployer (largely union) pension plans, especially those whose benefits had already been cut, and the contributing employers in those plans, whose obligations would be backstopped by federal money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees in failing union pension plans

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new PBGC 'special partition' program that assumes part of an eligible plan's liabilities so the plan stays solvent for 30 years with no cut in accrued benefits, funded by appropriations from the general fund with no repayment obligation for the plan.

Requires plans receiving partition aid to reinstate benefits that were suspended under prior federal approvals and to pay retirees the amounts previously cut, as a lump sum within 3 months or in monthly installments over 5 years.
Repeals the legal authority that let plans in critical and declining status suspend benefit payments (cuts already approved before enactment would stand).
Lets plans carry their prior-year funding status through 2020-2021 and extend their funding improvement or rehabilitation periods, to account for COVID-19 investment losses.
Raises the PBGC's guaranteed benefit formula for participants in insolvent multiemployer plans, with the rates indexed to average wages.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations from the general fund of the Treasury; the aid never has to be repaid and the government permanently assumes the transferred benefit liabilities.

drawbacks.text: The appropriation is open-ended ('such amounts as necessary'), the aid is not capped by the PBGC guarantee, and plans never have to repay it, leaving the total federal cost unbounded.
The PBGC may not condition aid on plan governance, its funding rules, or benefit levels, limiting federal oversight over how rescued plans are run.
Plans whose benefit cuts were already approved before enactment keep those cuts unless they qualify for partition aid, so relief would be uneven across retirees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For retirees facing 60-80 percent cuts to already-earned pensions, this is a powerful rescue, and the bill pairs it with real accountability tools: public reporting, GAO audits, an Inspector General budget, and a public application website. But the design is expensive and loose — unlimited appropriations, no repayment, no cap on assumed liabilities, and little federal control over plan management — so honest supporters have to acknowledge that the taxpayer bill is unknown and largely uncontrollable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 2021, with 42 senators as cosponsors — 40 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and both independents.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — is recorded for the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from this bill itself. Federal taxpayers were spared an open-ended, never-repaid appropriation, while retirees in failing multiemployer plans saw no relief through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers, not the retirees it targeted

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred; it sat from March 2021 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, with no Republican support on record, and the Democratic-chaired Finance Committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill makes federal money the permanent backstop keeping deeply underfunded union pension plans solvent for 30 years, converting a private pension promise into a federally funded one while keeping plan trustees in charge. For retirees, that means full benefits instead of deep cuts.

Federal aid relieves pressure for contribution increases and keeps plans from collapsing, though employers remain on the hook for withdrawal liability on partitioned amounts for 15 years after a partition.
The general fund would be tapped in unlimited, never-repaid amounts to cover plan liabilities, with the total cost left open-ended.
